items.prompt: Which choice correctly explains how the front and back covers of a closed book work?
choices: The back cover opens first, and the front cover closes the book.
The front cover opens first, and the back cover closes the book.
The spine opens first, and the back cover closes the book.
Both covers open first, and the spine closes the book.
items.answer: The front cover opens first, and the back cover closes the book.
items.rationale: The front cover is the side that opens first, while the back cover is on the opposite side and closes the book.

items.prompt: After reading one page of a storybook, what should the reader do to continue?
choices: Turn back to the previous page.
Close the book and choose another book.
Turn forward to the next page.
Fold the page and start reading again.
items.answer: Turn forward to the next page.
items.rationale: Readers continue a book by turning forward to the next page.

items.prompt: A page has a top row of words and a row below it. How should the reader read the page?
choices: Read left to right, then move down to the next row.
Read right to left, then move down to the next row.
Read left to right, then move up to the row above.
Read down each column before reading across the rows.
items.answer: Read left to right, then move down to the next row.
items.rationale: Reading moves from left to right across each row, then down to the next row.

items.prompt: What can the printed words on a card do for the person reading it?
items.rationale: Print conveys a message, allowing the reader to understand what the writer wants to say.

items.prompt: In a printed sentence, what separates one word from the next?
items.rationale: Words in print are separated by spaces so each word can be identified.

items.prompt: When beginning a line of print, where should a reader start?
items.rationale: English print is read from left to right, so a line begins at the left end.

items.prompt: Which part of a book usually gives its title and the names of the people who made it?
items.rationale: The title page usually displays the book’s title and identifies its author and illustrator.

items.prompt: Which part of a book is the outer cover a reader sees first?
items.rationale: The front cover is the outside cover facing the reader when the book is displayed.

items.prompt: Which part of a book often gives a short description of what the story is about?
items.rationale: The back cover often includes a brief description or summary of the book.

items.prompt: Which sentence correctly explains the jobs of the author and illustrator?
choices: The author writes the words, and the illustrator draws the pictures.
The author draws the pictures, and the illustrator writes the words.
The author reads the story, and the illustrator prints the pages.
The author cuts the pages, and the illustrator names the book.
items.answer: The author writes the words, and the illustrator draws the pictures.
items.rationale: An author writes the book’s words, while an illustrator creates the pictures that accompany them.

items.prompt: On a page, the word “Cat” is printed. Which letter position should you point to when finding the capital letter?
items.rationale: The capital C is the first letter of “Cat,” so that is the letter to point to.

items.prompt: A page reads: “I see my dog.” Which word position should you point to for the word after “see”?
items.rationale: The words are ordered I, see, my, dog, so the word after “see” is the third word.

items.prompt: A page reads: “The sun is warm. We go inside.” How many complete sentences are on the page?
items.rationale: “The sun is warm.” and “We go inside.” are two complete sentences.

items.prompt: How many claps match the syllable beats in “apple”?
items.rationale: “Apple” has two syllable beats, ap-ple, so two claps match the word.

items.prompt: Which syllable pattern should be clapped for “sunshine”?
items.rationale: “Sunshine” has two syllables, sun-shine, so each syllable represents one clap.

items.prompt: A learner wants to clap three beats for one word. Which word should they say?
items.rationale: “Tomato” has three syllables, to-ma-to, while each other choice has two syllables.

items.prompt: Which pair contains two words that each have two syllable beats?
items.rationale: “Lemon” and “rainbow” each have two syllables, so both words need two claps.

items.prompt: Say “The sun is hot” aloud. Tap once for each word you hear. How many taps should you make?
items.rationale: The sentence contains four words: The, sun, is, and hot. Tapping once for each word gives four taps.

items.prompt: Read each sentence aloud. Which sentence has exactly four words?
items.rationale: “The happy cat purrs.” has four words. The other sentences have three or five words.

items.prompt: Mia says “I see one cat” and taps three times. Is her tapping correct?
items.rationale: “I see one cat” contains four words, so Mia should tap four times rather than three.

items.prompt: Read each sentence aloud. Which sentence has fewer words than “A bright blue bird sings”?
items.rationale: The comparison sentence has five words. “Birds can sing well.” has four, so it has fewer words to tap.

items.prompt: Which word is made by blending the onset /m/ and the rime /op/?
items.rationale: Blending the starting sound /m/ with the ending chunk /op/ forms the word “mop.”

items.prompt: Which word can be split into the onset /d/ and the rime /og/?
items.rationale: The word “dog” splits into the starting sound /d/ and the ending chunk /og/.

items.prompt: Which sound is the onset in the word “jump”?
items.rationale: The onset is the word’s starting sound, which in “jump” is /j/.

items.prompt: Which chunk is the rime in the word “log”?
items.rationale: The rime is the ending chunk after the onset, so it is /og/ in “log.”

items.prompt: Which word rhymes with cat?
items.rationale: Hat and cat have the same ending sound, so they rhyme.

items.prompt: Complete the familiar rhyme: Twinkle, twinkle, little ___.
items.rationale: Star completes the familiar line “Twinkle, twinkle, little star.”

items.prompt: Which pair of words forms a rhyme?
items.rationale: Blue and shoe have matching ending sounds, so they rhyme.

items.prompt: Complete this song: The wheels on the bus go round and round, all through the ___.
items.rationale: Town completes the familiar song line “all through the town.”

items.prompt: What is the first sound you hear in the word “fish”?
items.rationale: The first sound in “fish” is /f/, so this choice is correct.

items.prompt: Which word starts with the /m/ sound?
items.rationale: “Moon” starts with the /m/ sound, while the other words start with different sounds.

items.prompt: Which pair of words begins with the same sound?
items.rationale: Both “bear” and “ball” begin with the /b/ sound.

items.prompt: Which word begins with a different first sound than the other three?
items.rationale: “Cat,” “cup,” and “car” begin with /k/, while “dog” begins with /d/.

items.prompt: Which word ends with the /m/ sound?
items.rationale: “Jam” ends with the /m/ sound. The other words end with /n/, /g/, and /p/.

items.prompt: Which word ends with the same sound as “cat”?
items.rationale: “Cat” and “hat” both end with the /t/ sound.

items.prompt: Which pair of words ends with the same sound?
items.rationale: “Mom” and “jam” both end with the /m/ sound.

items.prompt: Which word does not end with the /p/ sound?
items.rationale: “Dog” ends with the /g/ sound, while the other choices end with /p/.

items.prompt: Which sound is in the middle of the word cat?
items.rationale: Cat has three sounds: /k/–/ă/–/t/. The short a sound is in the middle.

items.prompt: Which word has the middle sound /ĕ/?
items.rationale: Hen has the sounds /h/–/ĕ/–/n/, so its middle sound is /ĕ/.

items.prompt: Which word has the same middle sound as cat?
items.rationale: Cat and map both have the short a sound, /ă/, in the middle.

items.prompt: A teacher is making a class list. Which word should the teacher write as a child’s first name?
items.rationale: Sofia is a child’s first name; the other choices are common words, not first names.

items.prompt: A child’s own name has three letters and begins and ends with A. Which name should the child find on a name tag?
items.rationale: Ana has three letters, and its first and last letters are A.

items.prompt: A family member’s name on a card has five letters and begins with G. Which name should the learner read?
items.rationale: Grace has five letters and begins with G.

items.prompt: Which word is written on the red, eight-sided road sign at an intersection?
items.rationale: STOP is the familiar word printed on red, eight-sided road signs.

items.prompt: A sign above a doorway in a public building says “EXIT.” What does that sign tell you?
items.rationale: EXIT marks a way out, so it tells a reader to go out through a door.

items.prompt: A grocery label names a round fruit that may be red or green. Which word is on the label?
items.rationale: APPLE is a familiar word on food labels and names a fruit that can be red or green.

items.prompt: Which word appears with the familiar yellow arches logo?
items.rationale: McDonald’s is the brand word shown with the familiar yellow arches logo.

items.prompt: Which word begins with the short a sound?
items.rationale: In “cat,” the letter a makes its short sound, /ă/.

items.prompt: Which word has the short e sound?
items.rationale: In “bed,” the letter e makes its short sound, /ĕ/.

items.prompt: Which two words use the short i and short o sounds?
items.rationale: “Pig” has the short i sound, and “dog” has the short o sound.

items.prompt: Which word ends with the short u sound?
items.rationale: In “cup,” the letter u makes its short sound, /ŭ/.

items.prompt: Say each word. Which word has a short e sound?
items.rationale: “Nest” has a short e sound. “Beach” has a long e sound, while “rain” and “train” have long a sounds.

items.prompt: Three words have short vowel sounds. Which word has a long vowel sound instead?
items.rationale: “Kite” has a long i sound. “Sock,” “fish,” and “duck” each have a short vowel sound.

items.prompt: Which pair contains two words with short vowel sounds?
items.rationale: “Pig” and “sun” both have short vowel sounds. Each of the other pairs has long vowel sounds.

items.prompt: Which letter makes the first sound in “bear”?
items.rationale: Bear begins with the /b/ sound, which is the sound made by B.

items.prompt: Which word begins with the /k/ sound?
items.rationale: Cake begins with the /k/ sound, which is the sound made by C.

items.prompt: Which letters make the first sounds in “dog” and “fish”?
items.rationale: Dog begins with the /d/ sound, and fish begins with the /f/ sound, so the letters are D and F.

items.prompt: Which word starts with the same sound as “goat”?
items.rationale: Girl starts with the /g/ sound, the same first sound as goat.

items.prompt: Which word starts with the H sound?
items.rationale: “Hat” begins with the /h/ sound, which is the sound linked to H.

items.prompt: Which letter matches the first sound in the word “jam”?
items.rationale: “Jam” begins with the /j/ sound, which is the sound linked to J.

items.prompt: Which word begins with the K sound?
items.rationale: “Kind” begins with the /k/ sound, which is the sound linked to K.

items.prompt: Which pair begins with the L sound and then the M sound?
items.rationale: “Leaf” begins with /l/ and “moon” begins with /m/, matching L and M in order.

items.prompt: Which word begins with the /n/ sound?
items.rationale: “Nest” begins with the /n/ sound, so it is the correct choice.

items.prompt: Which letter makes the first sound in “pear”?
items.rationale: “Pear” begins with the sound that the letter P makes.

items.prompt: Which word begins with the sound made by the letter Q?
items.rationale: “Quilt” begins with the /kw/ sound represented by Q.

items.prompt: Which pair of words begins with the sounds of R and S, in that order?
items.rationale: “Rose” begins with /r/ and “sun” begins with /s/, so they match the requested order.

items.prompt: Which word begins with the sound made by the letter T?
items.rationale: The letter T makes the /t/ sound, and “top” begins with that sound.

items.prompt: Which letter makes the same first sound as the word “van”?
items.rationale: The letter V makes the /v/ sound, which is heard at the start of “van.”

items.prompt: Which word starts with the /w/ sound?
items.rationale: The word “wet” begins with the /w/ sound made by the letter W.

items.prompt: Which letter stands for the /m/ sound?
items.rationale: The letter m is the code for the /m/ sound.

items.prompt: In the word “sun,” what sound does the first letter, s, stand for?
items.rationale: The letter s stands for the /s/ sound, which is the first sound in “sun.”

items.prompt: What does each letter tell us when we read?
items.rationale: Letters are codes for sounds, so they tell us what to say when reading.

items.prompt: Which word begins with the letter sound /p/?
items.rationale: The first letter in “pig” is p, which stands for the /p/ sound.

items.prompt: Which word is made by changing the /æ/ sound in “sat” to the /ɪ/ sound?
items.rationale: “Sit” is made by changing the middle /æ/ sound in “sat” to /ɪ/, while keeping the first and last sounds the same.

items.prompt: Which word is made by dropping the first sound from “cat”?
items.rationale: “At” is made by dropping the initial /k/ sound from “cat,” leaving the word “at.”

items.prompt: Which word is made by adding the /k/ sound to the beginning of “at”?
items.rationale: “Cat” is made by adding the initial /k/ sound to “at,” creating a new spoken word.

items.prompt: Which word is made by swapping the first and last sounds in “tap”?
items.rationale: “Pat” is made by swapping the first /t/ and last /p/ sounds in “tap,” while keeping the middle vowel the same.

items.prompt: Which word belongs to the first group of common sight words?
items.rationale: “The” is included in the first group of common sight words; the other choices are not.

items.prompt: Which sight word completes the sentence: “___ bird”?
items.rationale: “A bird” is correct, so the sight word “a” completes the sentence.

items.prompt: Which sight word completes the sentence: “Sam ___ here”?
items.rationale: “Sam is here” is correct, so “is” completes the sentence.

items.prompt: Which choice contains two first-group sight words?
items.rationale: Both “I” and “and” belong to the first group of common sight words.

items.prompt: Which word fits the sentence: “I gave ___ a book”?
items.rationale: “Them” names the people or things receiving the book. The other look-alike words do not fit the sentence.

items.prompt: We finished our game; ___ we went home.
items.rationale: “Then” shows that going home happened next or at that time.

items.prompt: ___ puppy is sleeping.
items.rationale: “The” identifies one particular puppy. The other look-alike words do not fit before the noun.

items.prompt: Which word has the letters t, h, e, n from left to right?
items.rationale: “Then” is spelled t-h-e-n. Each other choice has a different letter or letter order.

items.prompt: Which word completes the sentence: "I want ___ sing a song"?
items.rationale: “To” is needed before the verb “sing” in this sentence: “I want to sing a song.”

items.prompt: The box is red. Which word can replace "the box" in the sentence "The box is red"?
items.rationale: “It” refers to the single box already mentioned. “We” and “us” refer to groups, while “he” would refer to a person.

items.prompt: Which word describes something being inside a larger place or container?
items.rationale: “In” means inside a place or container. “On,” “at,” and “by” describe other positions or relationships.

items.prompt: Which pair matches these meanings: something belonging to the speaker, and the speaker together with other people?
items.rationale: “My” shows possession, and “we” includes the speaker together with other people.

items.prompt: A teacher tells this story: Mia put a red block in a box. Then she put a blue block on top. What color was the block on top?
items.rationale: The story says Mia put a blue block on top, so the block on top was blue.

items.prompt: A teacher tells this story: A dog ran after a ball into the park. A cat sat on a bench and watched. Who ran after the ball?
items.rationale: The story says the dog ran after the ball, while the cat sat on the bench.

items.prompt: A teacher tells this story: Sam and his mom baked cookies in the kitchen. Then they carried the cookies to the porch and ate them there. Which question asks about where the cookies were eaten?
choices: Where did they eat the cookies?
Who baked the cookies with Sam?
What did they bake in the kitchen?
When did they bake the cookies?
items.answer: Where did they eat the cookies?
items.rationale: This question asks about the place where the cookies were eaten, which is a key detail in the story.

items.prompt: A teacher tells this story: Niko heard a drum outside. He went to the window and saw three friends marching. What did Niko do after hearing the drum?
items.rationale: After hearing the drum, Niko went to the window and looked outside at his friends.

items.prompt: Which pair contains the word for the person spoken to and the word a speaker uses for himself or herself?
items.rationale: “You” refers to the person being spoken to, while “me” tells how a speaker refers to himself or herself.

items.prompt: Which sight word means to look with your eyes?
items.rationale: “See” means to look with your eyes; “sea” is a different word with the same sound.

items.prompt: Which sight word can mean to enjoy or be fond of something?
items.rationale: “Like” is used to say that something is enjoyed or pleasing.

items.prompt: Which sight word means to move or travel from one place to another?
items.rationale: “Go” means to move or travel from one place to another.

items.prompt: Before a read-aloud, a book cover shows a boy holding a red kite and looking up at a cloudy sky. What is the most likely event later in the story?
choices: The boy uses the kite to cover his lunch.
The boy finds his dog under the garden bench.
The boy watches his kite rise high into the sky.
The boy rides his kite all the way to school.
items.answer: The boy watches his kite rise high into the sky.
items.rationale: The cloudy sky and the boy holding a kite suggest that wind will lift the kite, so watching it rise is the most likely event.

items.prompt: During a read-aloud, you predict that the bear will sleep in a cave. The next page shows the bear lying on a blanket beside a tree. Which statement best checks your prediction?
choices: My guess was right because the bear lay down.
My guess was wrong because the bear was outside.
I should skip the book because my guess was wrong.
I should guess again before reading another page.
items.answer: My guess was wrong because the bear was outside.
items.rationale: The prediction can be checked by comparing it with the next page. The bear is beside a tree, not in a cave, so the guess was wrong.

items.prompt: A book cover shows a child planting a seed in soil. The story so far says the child waters it every day. What is the most likely event later in the story?
choices: The child moves the pot to a dark closet.
The child gives the seed to his best friend.
The child notices a small green sprout in the soil.
The child digs up the seed to see its color.
items.answer: The child notices a small green sprout in the soil.
items.rationale: A seed that is planted and watered is likely to grow, so finding a green sprout in the soil is the most reasonable prediction.

items.prompt: Mia put on rain boots and splashed through a puddle. Which detail in an illustration would show part of what the story tells?
choices: A child splashing through a puddle in rain boots
Empty boots standing beside a closed door
A child reading a book under a table
Rain falling on a dry and empty sidewalk
items.answer: A child splashing through a puddle in rain boots
items.rationale: The splashing child and rain boots visually show the action and important detail described in the story.

items.prompt: Lin built a tower of blocks, but it fell when he bumped the table. Which illustration detail would show part of this story?
choices: Blocks scattered on the floor beside a table
Blocks stacked neatly inside a basket
Lin carrying blocks toward a basket
A tall tower standing on the table
items.answer: Blocks scattered on the floor beside a table
items.rationale: Blocks scattered beside the table show the result of the tower falling, matching part of the story.

items.prompt: A fox was cold, so it curled up under a large tree. Which illustration detail would show part of the story?
choices: A curled-up fox beneath a large tree
A standing fox beside a small bush
A fox swimming across a pond
A fox walking toward a dark cave
items.answer: A curled-up fox beneath a large tree
items.rationale: The curled-up fox under the tree visually shows what the fox did and where it rested.

items.prompt: Nora could not see the moon because thick clouds covered it. Which illustration detail would show this part of the story?
choices: A round moon hidden behind thick clouds
A bright moon above scattered clouds
Round clouds beside a bright sun
A dark sky with stars and no clouds
items.answer: A round moon hidden behind thick clouds
items.rationale: A moon hidden behind clouds shows why Nora could not see it, illustrating the story detail.

items.prompt: Before a read-aloud about apples, Ana says, “I already know something about apples. I am not sure what the story will say.” Which response could tell Ana’s prior knowledge?
choices: The story may have a funny ending.
The read-aloud may show a tree.
I wonder who will tell the story.
items.rationale: Knowing that apples can grow on trees is information Ana brings to the read-aloud. The other choices express predictions, possibilities, or questions rather than prior knowledge.

items.prompt: During a read-aloud about folding a paper boat, Ben says, “I made a paper boat at school. I remember using paper and folding it. This part feels familiar.” What is Ben doing?
choices: Predicting what will happen after the story.
Comparing the book with a movie he saw.
Connecting the book to something he already did.
Learning a new word from the pictures.
items.answer: Connecting the book to something he already did.
items.rationale: Ben connects the read-aloud to his own experience of making a paper boat, showing how the book matches what he already knows.

items.prompt: Before a story about a robot dog, Kim says, “Real dogs bark.” The book then shows the robot dog staying quiet. Kim says, “That surprised me.” How did Kim connect her knowledge to the book?
choices: Using a new bark fact to predict the ending.
She used what she knew about real dogs to notice a difference.
Comparing two books about pets and finding one funny.
Remembering a place where she heard a loud sound.
items.answer: She used what she knew about real dogs to notice a difference.
items.rationale: Kim uses her existing knowledge that real dogs bark to recognize and describe the book’s surprising difference.

items.prompt: Noah read a book about building a birdhouse. He says, “My grandfather built one, so I know how making one feels. I was surprised by the blue roof.” Which statement best explains Noah’s talk?
choices: It makes a prediction and compares two different books.
It asks a question and repeats a fact from a movie.
It tells a new fact and wonders what will happen next.
It connects prior experience with a surprising book detail.
items.answer: It connects prior experience with a surprising book detail.
items.rationale: Noah connects building a birdhouse with his grandfather’s experience and identifies the blue roof as something surprising in the book.

items.prompt: Which book is a fact book?
choices: A book that explains how caterpillars change into butterflies
A book about a talking caterpillar looking for a friend
A book about a butterfly that visits a magic garden
A book about a girl who shares a butterfly garden
items.answer: A book that explains how caterpillars change into butterflies
items.rationale: This book gives true information about how caterpillars change into butterflies.

items.prompt: Which book is a storybook?
choices: A book that explains what makes rain
A book that lists kinds of clouds and their shapes
A book about a dragon who learns to help others
A book that describes how fish stay underwater
items.answer: A book about a dragon who learns to help others
items.rationale: The dragon’s adventure is a made-up story, so this is a storybook.

items.prompt: Read this sentence: “Whales are large animals that live in the ocean.” Which kind of book most likely contains it?
choices: A storybook about a whale’s pretend voyage
A funny book about a whale at school
A book about a lost whale in a swimming pool
A fact book about ocean animals
items.answer: A fact book about ocean animals
items.rationale: The sentence gives true information about whales, so it belongs in a fact book.

items.prompt: Why do readers use a fact book instead of a storybook?
choices: To follow a made-up character’s adventures
To learn true information about a topic
To hear about problems that never happened
To learn how a pretend world is created
items.answer: To learn true information about a topic
items.rationale: A fact book provides true information about real topics, while a storybook tells a made-up story.

items.prompt: A teacher read aloud: “Niko took a book from a shelf. He read two pages. He smiled and shut the book.” Which retelling tells the events in the right order?
choices: Took a book, read pages, then shut it.
Read pages, took a book, then shut it.
Took a book, shut it, then read pages.
Shut a book, took a book, then read pages.
items.answer: Took a book, read pages, then shut it.
items.rationale: Niko first took a book, next read two pages, and last smiled and shut the book.

items.prompt: A teacher read: “Leo found a seed. He planted it in soil. He watered it. Soon a green plant appeared.” Which event happened next after Leo planted the seed?
items.rationale: After planting the seed, Leo watered it, so water falling onto the seed was the next event.

items.prompt: A teacher read: “A rabbit was inside its burrow. It hopped outside. It spotted a carrot. It ate the carrot. Then it returned underground.” Which event happened first?
choices: The rabbit stayed inside its burrow
items.answer: The rabbit stayed inside its burrow
items.rationale: The rabbit was inside its burrow before hopping outside, finding the carrot, eating it, and returning underground.

items.prompt: A teacher sings a familiar verse and invites everyone to sing the next part. What should you do?
choices: Sing the words along with the teacher
Watch the teacher without making a sound
Sing different words that you invent
Ask to leave the singing circle
items.answer: Sing the words along with the teacher
items.rationale: Singing the words along with the teacher is directly joining in and repeating the poem or song.

items.prompt: During a chant, the teacher says, “Tap your knees on this word.” How can you join in?
choices: Tap your knees and say the repeated word
Cover your ears while the class is chanting
Say the words without tapping your knees
Start a new chant after the teacher stops
items.answer: Tap your knees and say the repeated word
items.rationale: Tapping your knees and saying the repeated word shows coordinated participation in the chant.

items.prompt: After hearing a favourite nursery rhyme, how can you show that you enjoyed it?
choices: Smile and sing along with the rhyme
Walk away and say nothing at all
Read the words silently to yourself
Tell everyone that you dislike it
items.answer: Smile and sing along with the rhyme
items.rationale: Smiling and singing along are clear ways of showing enjoyment and joining in with a favourite rhyme.

items.prompt: Your classmates begin singing the refrain of a song. What can you do to join them?
choices: Sing the refrain after your classmates
Speak quietly while they are singing
Sing only when nobody is listening
Stop singing before the refrain begins
items.answer: Sing the refrain after your classmates
items.rationale: Singing the refrain after classmates joins the group in repeating the song.

items.prompt: A chant says: “Row, row, row your boat. Gently down the stream. Row, row, row your boat. Merrily we go.” How many times can learners join in with the repeated line?
items.rationale: The chant contains two instances of “Row, row, row your boat,” so learners can join in with that line twice.

items.prompt: The class reads: “Tick tock, little clock. Tick tock, little clock.” What should the learners do when the repeated line comes around again?
choices: Say it together with the class
Say it only in a whisper
items.answer: Say it together with the class
items.rationale: Joining in with a repeated line means saying the same line along with the class or teacher.

items.prompt: A poem begins: “I see a little cat with a hat.” Which word should come next to rhyme with “hat”?
items.rationale: “Bat” and “hat” have the same short a sound, so “bat” completes the rhyme.

items.prompt: Which word ends with the same sound as “kit”?
items.rationale: “Sit” and “kit” both end with the same short i sound.

items.prompt: An adult reads two frog books aloud. The first says frogs have webbed feet. The second says frogs can leap far with strong back legs. Which idea combines what both books add?
choices: Frogs have webbed feet and strong back legs.
Frogs have webbed feet but cannot leap.
Frogs have smooth skin and strong back legs.
Frogs live near water and eat insects.
items.answer: Frogs have webbed feet and strong back legs.
items.rationale: The correct choice combines the new detail from each book: webbed feet from the first and strong back legs from the second.

items.prompt: An adult reads three books about trucks. One shows a dump truck carrying sand, one a tow truck moving a car, and one a fire truck carrying water. What do the books add to the child's knowledge of trucks?
choices: Trucks can have different jobs and carry different things.
Trucks all carry sand and perform the same job.
Tow trucks carry water while dump trucks move cars.
Every truck is red and works at a fire station.
items.answer: Trucks can have different jobs and carry different things.
items.rationale: The correct choice shows what the books collectively add: trucks perform different jobs and carry different things.

items.prompt: After listening to frog books, a child knows frogs lay eggs, tadpoles grow legs, and adult frogs hop. Which detail would add to the child's understanding of a frog's life cycle?
choices: Frogs begin as eggs, become tadpoles, then become adult frogs.
Tadpoles hatch with legs and never change afterward.
Frogs begin as adult frogs and later become eggs.
Only tadpoles can swim, and adult frogs cannot.
items.answer: Frogs begin as eggs, become tadpoles, then become adult frogs.
items.rationale: The correct choice adds the order of a frog's life cycle: egg, tadpole, and adult frog.

items.prompt: Four books are about apples. One explains how apples grow, one shows apple varieties, one describes ways people use apples, and one teaches an apple song. What do these books together help a child notice?
choices: One topic can be explored in several different ways.
Apples have only one variety and one use.
Songs are the best way to learn how apples grow.
Every book about apples gives the same facts.
items.answer: One topic can be explored in several different ways.
items.rationale: The correct choice explains that several books can explore the same topic by adding different kinds of information.

items.prompt: Dr. Seuss wrote The Cat in the Hat and The Cat in the Hat Comes Back. What do the books have in common?
choices: They both feature the same mischievous Cat character.
They both feature a child beginning a school day.
They both include a dog who helps the Cat.
They both show the Cat cooking a large meal.
items.answer: They both feature the same mischievous Cat character.
items.rationale: The Cat in the Hat and The Cat in the Hat Comes Back both feature the same mischievous Cat character.

items.prompt: The Very Hungry Caterpillar eats many foods. The Grumpy Caterpillar feels itchy and dislikes his bed. Which comparison is correct?
choices: One seeks food; the other seeks itch relief.
One stays hungry; the other feels sleepy.
One eats many foods; the other eats once.
One has friends; the other has no friends.
items.answer: One seeks food; the other seeks itch relief.
items.rationale: The Very Hungry Caterpillar focuses on finding food, while The Grumpy Caterpillar focuses on escaping the discomfort of an itchy bed.

items.prompt: Bill Martin Jr. wrote Brown Bear, Brown Bear, What Do You See? and Polar Bear, Polar Bear, What Do You See? Which animals begin the books’ patterns?
choices: A brown bear, then a polar bear.
A polar bear, then a brown bear.
A red bird, then a white seal.
A blue horse, then a green tree.
items.answer: A brown bear, then a polar bear.
items.rationale: Brown Bear, Brown Bear, What Do You See? begins with a brown bear, and Polar Bear, Polar Bear, What Do You See? begins with a polar bear.

items.prompt: Margaret Wise Brown wrote Goodnight Moon, and Peggy Rathmann wrote Goodnight Gorilla. Which statement compares the books correctly?
choices: Goodnight Moon follows a child; Goodnight Gorilla follows a zoo gorilla.
Goodnight Moon follows a zoo; Goodnight Gorilla follows a school child.
Goodnight Moon ends at sunrise; Goodnight Gorilla ends after breakfast.
Both books follow a baby saying goodnight around a room.
items.answer: Goodnight Moon follows a child; Goodnight Gorilla follows a zoo gorilla.
items.rationale: Goodnight Moon centers on a child going to bed, while Goodnight Gorilla centers on a gorilla saying goodnight in a zoo.

items.prompt: While reading a simple pattern book, a child should do which pair of actions?
choices: Read each line and point to every word.
Read only favorite lines and point to pictures.
Read silently and point to one word per page.
Read each line and point only to new words.
items.answer: Read each line and point to every word.
items.rationale: Reading each line while pointing to every word shows the learner is reading for meaning and tracking the print.

items.prompt: Before reading a simple pattern book, what should the learner do to read with purpose?
choices: Look at the cover and title and think about the story.
Close the book and wait for an adult to explain it.
Count all the pages without looking at the words.
Read the last page first to find the ending.
items.answer: Look at the cover and title and think about the story.
items.rationale: Looking at the cover and title helps the learner think about what the book may be about before reading.

items.prompt: The first line of a pattern book says, “I see a cat.” Which word should the learner point to first?
items.rationale: English print is read from left to right, so the learner points to “I” first and then continues through each word.

items.prompt: A child skips a word while reading a patterned sentence. What should the child do next?
choices: Go back, point to the missed word, and continue reading.
Keep going, then point to that word at the end.
Point to the next word and skip the missed one.
Close the book and choose another page.
items.answer: Go back, point to the missed word, and continue reading.
items.rationale: Returning to the missed word and pointing to it helps the learner keep track of every word and continue reading purposefully.

items.prompt: Which action best shows a child looking through a book independently?
choices: The child turns the pages and looks at each part carefully.
The child asks an adult to read every page aloud.
The child closes the book after seeing only the cover.
The child waits for an adult to turn every page.
items.answer: The child turns the pages and looks at each part carefully.
items.rationale: Turning the pages and examining the book shows that the child is looking through it without relying on an adult.

items.prompt: Lena enjoyed a book about cats and wants to pick another book she may like. Which choice best shows using her own interests?
choices: Choose another book about cats from the book shelf.
Choose a book about cats because her teacher ordered it.
Choose a book about trains without looking at her interest.
Choose a book she has not seen because it is the nearest.
items.answer: Choose another book about cats from the book shelf.
items.rationale: Selecting another cat book shows that Lena is using what she enjoyed to make her own choice.

items.prompt: Which comment best shows a child talking about a book they enjoyed?
choices: I liked the funny part about the lost dog.
The dog book has a green cover.
I found the dog book on the shelf.
The dog book is longer than my other books.
items.answer: I liked the funny part about the lost dog.
items.rationale: The child identifies a part of the story and says they liked it, showing both enjoyment and talking about the book.

items.prompt: Which action best shows a child choosing a book to read again?
choices: Picking the book they enjoyed and opening it again.
Picking a book they have never seen before.
Picking a book because it has the most pages.
Picking a book because an adult chose it.
items.answer: Picking the book they enjoyed and opening it again.
items.rationale: Choosing a previously enjoyed book and opening it again shows independent selection based on personal enjoyment.
